summary: Djibouti lies in the Horn of Africa and controls the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. It became independent from France in 1977 and is an important international port and the site of the military bases of many countries.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Djibouti lies beside the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the mouth of the Red Sea; from the 7th century Arab merchants came here to trade via the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and Islam was introduced with them. In the 14th–16th centuries the Adal Sultanate, centered on the nearby port of Zeila, fully Islamized the local Somalis (the Issa clan) and the Afar, who follow the Shafi‘i school of Sunni Islam. Islam is the shared identity of the two major peoples, and the constitution also designates Islam as the state religion.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: France purchased Obock in 1862 and from the 1880s established French Somaliland; Catholic missions came with colonization, but very few local residents converted. The Djibouti–Addis Ababa railway, opened in 1917, attracted Ethiopians to settle and brought Ethiopian Orthodoxy; today Christians are mainly residents of Ethiopian origin, European expatriates and military personnel.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: These include Hinduism brought by Indian merchants and the other faiths of foreign garrisons and expatriates. Djibouti hosts overseas bases of France, the United States, China, Japan and other countries, and the foreign population is highly fluid, but the number of long-settled non-Muslims is very small.

religion.background: Djibouti has been a way station for Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade since antiquity; Islam arrived by sea in the early Islamic era and became deeply rooted in Somali and Afar society during the medieval Adal Sultanate. French colonization in the late 19th century brought Catholicism, and the opening of the railway in the early 20th century attracted Orthodox Ethiopians. After independence in 1977 Islam became the core of national identity, while the constitution guarantees freedom of religion, and the garrisons and immigrants of various countries make up the minority religious groups.

language.official: French and Arabic are the official languages.

ranking.name: Somali
ranking.description: Somali is the mother tongue of Somalis such as the Issa clan, who live mainly in the capital and the south and are the most numerous, so Somali is the language most often heard on the street. In 1972 neighboring Somalia devised a Latin-alphabet orthography for Somali, which promoted its written use; in Djibouti it is a national language, widely used in broadcasting and everyday commerce.

ranking.name: Afar
ranking.description: The Afar live in the north and west and are part of the nomadic “Afar Triangle” people spanning Ethiopia and Eritrea. In the colonial period France called the territory the “French Territory of the Afars and the Issas” (1967–1977), reflecting the coexistence of the two major groups; in 1991–1994 an armed Afar insurgency fought a civil war with the government, and the balance of language and ethnicity remains a political issue to this day.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Djibouti faces the Arabian Peninsula across the sea, Yemeni merchants have long settled here, and Islamic education is also conducted in Arabic. At independence in 1977 Arabic was made one of the official languages and Djibouti joined the Arab League, but those whose mother tongue is Arabic are mainly the Yemeni-origin community.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: France ruled here from acquiring Obock in 1862 and founding Djibouti City in 1888 until independence in 1977. French therefore remains an official language and dominates government, law and schooling, but most people learn it as a second language, and few have French as a mother tongue.

language.history: Djibouti’s two major indigenous languages, Somali and Afar, both belong to the Cushitic branch of the Afroasiatic family, each corresponding to one of the two major peoples. After the arrival of Islam, Arabic became the language of religion and commerce. With French colonization in the late 19th century, French became the language of administration and education; after independence in 1977 French and Arabic became co-official languages, while Somali and Afar are recognized as national languages. Today most Djiboutians can switch between their mother tongue, French and Arabic.

ranking.name: Skoudehkaris
ranking.description: Rice is cooked together with lamb or goat meat, with tomato, onion and spices such as cardamom, cumin and clove, giving a rich aroma, and it is often eaten with banana.
ranking.history: This dish is regarded as Djibouti’s national dish; its spiced rice reflects the long influence of Yemeni and Indian food culture on Djibouti as a Red Sea trading port, as the rice and spices were mostly goods imported by sea. The sheep raised by the local nomads supply the main meat. It is sure to be served at Eid al-Fitr, weddings and other occasions, and is the signature dish for entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Lahoh
ranking.description: Flour is fermented with a starter and then fried on a griddle into a thin pancake covered in air holes, soft with a slight sourness, often drizzled with honey or ghee and eaten for breakfast.
ranking.history: Lahoh originated in Yemen; the long-standing exchange between Yemen and the Horn of Africa across the Bab-el-Mandeb made this fermented flatbread common in Djibouti and Somalia, where it is called laxoox or canjeero in Somali. It is similar to Ethiopian injera but thinner and smaller. Djiboutians often have it for breakfast with sweet milk tea, and also tear it up to dip in stew or soup, making it one of the most common everyday staples.

ranking.name: Fah-fah
ranking.description: A spicy clear soup stewed from goat or lamb with potato, carrot, chili and garlic, with a fresh, hot broth, often eaten with fermented flatbread.
ranking.history: Fah-fah is a home-style soup unique to Djibouti, reflecting the local nomads’ way of life based on raising goats and sheep, where a single pot of meat soup can feed a whole family. In the hot, dry climate, a hot soup with chili is thought to stimulate the appetite and restore energy. It often appears at family gatherings and at the breaking of the fast in Ramadan and is one of the soups most representative of Djibouti in people’s minds.

ranking.name: Sambusa
ranking.description: Thin dough is wrapped around seasoned minced beef or lamb, onion, green chili and spices, folded into a triangle and deep-fried until the shell is golden and crisp.
ranking.history: The ancestor of the sambusa is the medieval Persian and Arab “sanbusak,” which spread to East Africa and India through Indian Ocean trade networks, with different versions developing in each place. Djibouti’s version blends Arab and Indian spices. It is most closely associated with Ramadan, when households everywhere prepare it for the sunset breaking of the fast, and it is also a common snack on the street and in cafés.

ranking.name: Xalwo (halwa)
ranking.description: A translucent, jelly-like sweet cooked from sugar, cornstarch, ghee, cardamom and nutmeg, chewy and richly aromatic.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Arabic “halwa” (sweet); such sweets reached the Horn of Africa through the trade networks of the Arab and Ottoman worlds, and Somalis developed a distinctive version cooked from starch and ghee. Because it requires long stirring, it is traditionally made only for festivals such as weddings, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, and is served to guests with coffee or tea.
